businesses.pitch: A giant airport terminal where planes from all over the world land and take off.
businesses.earns: Airlines pay a fee for every plane that lands and every passenger they carry. Shops and cafés pay rent, and the car park earns too.
businesses.costs: Security staff and scanners, runway and terminal repairs, power, baggage belts, fire crews, and paying back the huge building loan.
businesses.risks: Fog and storms that cancel flights, an airline moving to a rival airport, a security scare, broken baggage belts and quiet winters.
businesses.tip: Airports sell smooth journeys: short queues, bags that arrive and planes that leave on time keep airlines and travellers coming.

cases.title: Opening the new terminal
cases.story: Your $60 million terminal opens in spring. Three big airlines want gates (the doors where planes park and passengers board). A shop company wants to run every shop for a fixed rent, and you need 400 trained security staff before the summer rush.

options.text: Give each airline gates, with fees that drop as they add more flights
options.result: All three airlines sign, and two add extra routes to earn the lower fee. By summer your departures board is full from dawn till midnight.
options.lesson: A deal that rewards customers for growing makes them want to grow with you.

options.text: Hire and train all 400 security staff well before the first flight
options.result: Training takes three months, but on opening day everyone moves through security quickly and calmly. Travellers post photos of friendly staff, not long queues.
options.lesson: Well-trained people make a busy place feel calm and safe.

options.text: Let the shops pay a share of their sales instead of a fixed rent
options.result: When the summer crowds arrive, the shops sell more and so do you. You pick shops travellers love: local food, books and toys.
options.lesson: When you share in your partners' sales, you both want the same thing: more happy shoppers.

options.text: Insure the terminal against fires, floods and storm damage
options.result: The cover costs millions every year, which stings. But if a storm ever floods the baggage hall, you won't have to pay for it all yourself.
options.lesson: For a business this big, insurance is a small, sure cost that guards against a giant one.

options.text: Charge airlines the highest fees in the country: they need you
options.result: Two airlines move their flights to a rival airport along the coast. Empty gates earn nothing at all.
options.lesson: Customers who can go elsewhere will, if your price isn't fair.

cases.title: A drone near the runway
cases.story: On a busy Friday evening, air traffic controller Sofia spots a drone (a small flying camera) near the runway. A drone hitting a plane could be very dangerous. Thirty planes are waiting, and the airlines warn that every hour of delay costs them a fortune.

options.text: Keep the planes flying: it's probably just a toy
options.result: A landing plane passes very close to the drone. Nobody is hurt, but the air safety authority fines you heavily and the story is on every news channel.
options.lesson: When safety is in doubt, stop and check: no timetable is worth the risk.

options.text: Pause flights, call the police drone team and update travellers
options.result: Police find the drone's owner in a nearby field within the hour. Flights restart safely, and travellers thank you for the clear updates.
options.lesson: In an emergency, follow the safety rules quickly and keep people informed.

options.text: Buy a drone-spotting radar that finds drones and their pilots fast
options.result: The next time a drone appears, the radar spots it in seconds and shows police where its pilot is standing. The delay lasts minutes, not hours.
options.lesson: If a problem could happen again, invest in a faster way to deal with it.

options.text: Give waiting travellers free water, snacks and phone charging
options.result: Waiting is still boring, but families feel looked after. Many write kind reviews about your staff instead of angry ones.
options.lesson: When you can't stop a delay, you can still make the wait kinder.

options.text: Tell travellers nothing until the drone has gone
options.result: Thousands of travellers stare at a board that just says 'delayed'. Rumours fly online, and by bedtime angry posts are everywhere.
options.lesson: When people are kept in the dark, they imagine the worst.

cases.title: Parcel planes at night
cases.story: A parcel company wants to fly 20 cargo planes from your airport every night, paying $1 million a month. But the planes are loud, and 5,000 families live near the runway. The council's noise meters record every take-off, and too much noise means big fines.

options.text: Agree, but only quieter new planes, and none from 1am to 5am
options.result: The parcel company sends its quietest planes and plans around the quiet hours. Families sleep, parcels fly, and your income jumps.
options.lesson: The best deals find a way for everyone to win, even the neighbours.

options.text: Pay to fit thick, quiet windows in the homes nearest the runway
options.result: Workers fit extra-thick windows in 800 homes near the runway. Families say they now sleep better than before the airport grew.
options.lesson: When your business affects your neighbours, help them first and they'll support you.

options.text: Write in the contract that they pay any fines for noisy planes
options.result: In the first week, one old plane breaks the noise limit. The parcel company pays the fine, just as the contract says.
options.lesson: Agree who pays for problems before the problems happen.

options.text: Switch the noise meters off at night so the fines never come
options.result: A neighbour notices the meters go dark every night and tells the council. You're fined millions, and night flights are banned completely.
options.lesson: Hiding a problem from the people who check it makes it far worse when they find out.

options.text: Say no: night flights are more trouble than they're worth
options.result: The parcel company takes its planes, and its $1 million a month, to a rival airport. Your runway sits empty all night.
options.lesson: Saying no to every tricky deal means missing the ones you could have made work.

businesses.pitch: A grand harbour terminal where giant cruise ships full of holidaymakers dock.
businesses.earns: Cruise lines pay a fee for every ship that docks and every passenger. Shops, coach trips and the car park bring in more money.
businesses.costs: Port staff and security, keeping the harbour deep enough, cleaning, coaches, insurance and paying back the loan for the terminal.
businesses.risks: Storms that send ships elsewhere, a cruise line choosing a rival port, illness spreading on a ship, and quiet winters with few visitors.
businesses.tip: Each ship brings a small town of visitors at once: make their day ashore easy and fun, and the cruise lines will keep coming back.

cases.title: Ten thousand visitors a day
cases.story: Your $40 million cruise terminal opens next summer. On busy days, two ships could bring 10,000 visitors before breakfast. The cruise lines ask: can everyone get ashore within an hour? The town's shops ask: will the visitors come to us, or stay by the ships?

options.text: Build plenty of check-in desks and a covered walkway into the old town
options.result: Passengers stroll ashore in minutes and straight into the old town. The shops are busy, and the cruise lines put your port on next year's routes.
options.lesson: Make it easy for customers to arrive and enjoy themselves, and they'll come back.

options.text: Team up with local guides to sell coach trips and walking tours
options.result: Visitors explore castles, beaches and markets with friendly local guides. You earn a share of every trip, and the town welcomes the business.
options.lesson: Partners who know the area can sell experiences you couldn't create alone.

options.text: Hire staff who speak the languages of your visitors
options.result: Visitors from Spain, Japan and Brazil are greeted in their own language. Reviews mention the friendly welcome again and again.
options.lesson: Speaking your customers' language, even a little, makes them feel at home.

options.text: Insure the terminal against storms and floods
options.result: By the sea, storms are part of life. When a winter gale floods the arrivals hall, the insurer pays for the clean-up.
options.lesson: A small yearly cost that protects you from one big, unlucky night is money well spent.

options.text: Keep visitors in your terminal shops so they spend their money there
options.result: Visitors buy a few souvenirs but feel stuck. The town's shopkeepers complain, and online reviews say there's 'nothing to see here'.
options.lesson: Grabbing all the money for yourself can spoil the trip for everyone, including you.

cases.title: A typhoon is coming
cases.story: A typhoon (a giant tropical storm) will hit the coast in two days. A cruise ship with 4,000 passengers is due tomorrow and would still be in port when the storm arrives. The cruise line hates changing plans, and its captain asks for your advice.

options.text: Say the storm will probably miss, so nobody cancels
options.result: The typhoon arrives early, and the ship is stuck in port. Passengers wait out the storm in a crowded terminal, and the cruise line wants millions back.
options.lesson: Hiding bad news to protect sales puts people at risk and costs more in the end.

options.text: Help the ship switch to a safe port, and offer a free visit later
options.result: The ship sails to a calm port up the coast. Its passengers get a free visit next season, and the cruise line thanks you for the early warning.
options.lesson: Put safety first, then find a way to make it up to your customers.

options.text: Tie down cranes and walkways, and move everything loose indoors
options.result: The typhoon howls all night, but nothing blows loose. Two days later your terminal is ready for ships while other ports are still clearing up.
options.lesson: A storm plan practised before the storm is worth more than any repair.

options.text: Send passengers clear updates in their own languages
options.result: Passengers know exactly what is happening and why. Even those whose plans changed say they felt safe and well looked after.
options.lesson: In a crisis, clear and honest updates calm people down.

options.text: Close the terminal for a whole week, just to be extra safe
options.result: The storm passes in a day, but your terminal stays shut for six more. Two ships go to a rival port instead.
options.lesson: Being careful is wise; staying closed long after the danger has passed is not.

cases.title: The biggest ship in the world
cases.story: The world's biggest cruise ship, carrying 9,000 people, wants to visit every week. Your berth (a ship's parking spot) is too short, and making it longer costs $6 million. On her first visit, her owners ask your inspector to sign her fire-safety form without checking: 'We're late!'

options.text: Lengthen the berth in return for a 10-year visiting deal
options.result: The cruise line signs for ten years, so the longer berth pays for itself many times over. Every Saturday, 9,000 visitors pour into town.
options.lesson: Invest big when a long contract makes sure the money comes back.

options.text: Do the fire check properly, even if the ship leaves late
options.result: Your inspector finds a blocked fire door on deck 9, and it's cleared in an hour. The captain admits it: 9,000 people are now safer.
options.lesson: A safety check only works if you never skip it, especially when people are in a hurry.

options.text: Sign the form: such a famous ship must be safe
options.result: A week later, inspectors in another port find blocked fire doors and broken alarms. Your signature is on the form, so your port is fined and in the news.
options.lesson: Never sign that something is safe unless you have checked it yourself.

options.text: Plan with the town for 9,000 visitors: buses, toilets and guides
options.result: The town adds extra buses and pop-up help desks. The first giant visit goes smoothly, and the shops have their best Saturday ever.
options.lesson: When something big is coming, plan it with everyone it affects.

options.text: Charge the giant ship double: its owners can afford it
options.result: The cruise line says no and takes its giant ship to a rival port with fair prices. You get nothing at all.
options.lesson: A greedy price can lose you the whole deal.

businesses.pitch: A huge yard by the sea where welders and engineers build and repair giant ships.
businesses.earns: Ferry, cargo and cruise companies pay millions for each new ship, and pay again when their ships come in for repairs.
businesses.costs: Steel, engines, skilled welders and engineers, giant cranes, the dry dock where ships are built, safety gear, power and insurance.
businesses.risks: Late steel, a ship that costs more than planned, a worker hurt on the job, a buyer who can't pay, and fewer orders when trade slows.
businesses.tip: Ships take years to build, so check every buyer can pay, get paid in stages, and never rush the welding or the safety checks.

cases.title: The first big order
cases.story: A ferry company orders two new ferries from your shipyard for $35 million each, to be ready in three years. You need 600 skilled workers and tonnes of steel. The ferry company wants to pay only when each ship is finished, but your manager, Bogdan, says wages are due every week.

options.text: Agree a price paid in stages: at the start, halfway and on delivery
options.result: The ferry company pays a third at the start, a third halfway and the rest on delivery. You never have to pay wages from an empty bank account.
options.lesson: On a long job, get paid in stages so you never run out of cash halfway.

options.text: Train young apprentices (learners) as welders and engineers
options.result: Fifty school-leavers learn to weld and wire ships alongside your experts. Two years later they're skilled workers, and the town is proud of them.
options.lesson: Training young people is how a skilled business keeps its skills for the future.

options.text: Fix the price of your steel now with a long deal from a trusted supplier
options.result: Steel prices jump the next year, but you keep paying the agreed price. Both ferries stay on budget.
options.lesson: When your biggest cost can jump, fixing its price early protects your profit.

options.text: Check the ferry company's accounts before you sign
options.result: Its accounts are healthy, and it has paid every past shipyard on time. Now you can sign with confidence.
options.lesson: Before you spend years building for someone, make sure they can pay.

options.text: Promise both ferries in two years instead of three to win the order
options.result: Your team works flat out but still finishes late. The contract makes you pay for every late week, and the profit disappears.
options.lesson: Promising more than you can do turns a good order into a costly one.

cases.title: The safety inspection
cases.story: Safety inspectors visit on Monday. Your supervisor, Ruth, admits that some welders work high up on the ship without safety harnesses, because they say harnesses slow them down. The ship is due out next month, and its buyer is impatient.

options.text: Make everyone wear harnesses on Monday, just for the inspectors
options.result: The inspectors come back without warning on Thursday and find the same problem. They close the yard for two weeks and fine you heavily.
options.lesson: Safety is for every day, not just the day the inspector visits.

options.text: Stop all high-up work today until everyone has a harness that fits
options.result: Work pauses for two days while new, lighter harnesses arrive. The inspectors praise your quick action, and the welders say the new ones hardly slow them at all.
options.lesson: Fix a safety problem the moment you know about it, not the moment someone checks.

options.text: Ask the welders why they skip harnesses, and fix what bothers them
options.result: The welders explain that the straps catch on the scaffolding. Moving the safety lines fixes it, and now everyone clips on.
options.lesson: When people break a rule, ask why: the answer often shows you how to fix it.

options.text: Tell the buyer honestly that safety comes first, even if it's late
options.result: The buyer grumbles, then admits it would never want a ship built by people taking risks. It agrees to wait an extra week.
options.lesson: Good customers respect a company that won't cut corners.

options.text: Fine any welder caught without a harness, without asking why
options.result: Welders feel bullied and hide from supervisors instead of clipping on. The real problem, straps that snag, is never fixed.
options.lesson: Punishing people without listening rarely solves a safety problem.

cases.title: Clean ships and cheap steel
cases.story: A shipping company wants six cargo ships that run on clean fuel instead of oil: your biggest order ever. Your yard has never built one. Meanwhile a new supplier offers steel at a third off, with quality certificates (papers saying it's strong) that look a little smudged.

options.text: Build one ship first with the engine maker's experts, then the rest
options.result: The first clean ship takes a little longer, but your team learns every trick. The next five are faster and cheaper, and new orders roll in.
options.lesson: When you try something new, learn on the first one before you build the rest.

options.text: Buy the cheaper steel: the certificates say it's strong enough
options.result: Tests on the first hull show the steel cracks far too easily, and the certificates were fakes. Cutting it out and starting again costs millions.
options.lesson: Check that safety papers are real, especially on a deal that looks too cheap.

options.text: Send a sample of the cheap steel to a testing lab first
options.result: The lab finds the steel is much weaker than its papers claim. You report the supplier and stick with your trusted one.
options.lesson: When a deal is suspiciously cheap, test it before you trust it.

options.text: Ask the shipping company to help pay for learning something new
options.result: The shipping company agrees to pay extra for the first ship, because it wants the clean ships to work. You share the risk of going first.
options.lesson: When a customer wants something brand new, it's fair to share the cost of learning.

options.text: Say no: you only build the old kind of ship
options.result: A rival yard wins the order and learns to build clean ships. A few years later every buyer wants them, and the rival gets the orders.
options.lesson: When your customers' world is changing, learning the new way keeps you in business.

businesses.pitch: Sleek, super-fast trains that zoom between big cities at 300 kilometres an hour.
businesses.earns: Passengers buy tickets, and business travellers pay extra for quiet carriages. Cafés and shops in your stations pay rent too.
businesses.costs: Drivers and crew, electricity, repairs to tracks and trains, signals, station staff, safety checks and repaying the huge loans.
businesses.risks: Snow or storms on the line, a signal fault stopping every train, cheap flights tempting passengers away, and trains running late.
businesses.tip: On a fast railway, being on time is the product: check the track every night, and passengers will choose you over flying.

cases.title: Planning the route
cases.story: Your bullet train line will join two cities 400 kilometres apart. The straight route cuts through an ancient forest; going round it adds 10 minutes and costs more. To win passengers, your trains must beat the plane: one hour in the air, plus airport queues.

options.text: Go round the forest, and put stations right in each city centre
options.result: The forest is saved, and your trains still beat flying, because your stations are in the city centres while the airports are far out of town.
options.lesson: Think about your customers' whole journey, not just the fastest part.

options.text: Dig a tunnel under the forest: dearer, but straight and fast
options.result: The tunnel takes a year longer and costs a fortune, but the forest above is untouched and the trains are even faster.
options.lesson: The expensive answer can be worth it, as long as you can afford it.

options.text: Sell cheap tickets to early bookers and dearer ones on the day
options.result: Early bookers grab bargains and fill the quieter trains, while last-minute travellers pay more. Every train runs fuller.
options.lesson: Different prices for different times can fill empty seats without losing money.

options.text: Ask both cities to share the cost, since the line helps them grow
options.result: Both cities agree to pay for their own stations. Your loan is smaller, and the two mayors become your biggest fans.
options.lesson: When a project helps a whole region, partners will often share the cost.

options.text: Build straight through the forest: faster is all that matters
options.result: Protesters camp in the trees for months, the council delays your permission, and the 'forest-wrecking railway' is in every newspaper.
options.lesson: The quickest route isn't quickest if it makes everyone fight you.

cases.title: A crack in the rail
cases.story: At 5am, track engineer Isla finds a crack in one rail. The first train, carrying 900 people, leaves at six, and fixing the rail takes three hours. The control room says: 'Can't it wait until tonight? Our trains are never late!'

options.text: Run the morning trains on time and fix the crack tonight
options.result: The crack grows, and a driver has to brake hard. Nobody is hurt, but inspectors stop the whole line for a week and fine you heavily.
options.lesson: A timetable is never worth risking people's safety.

options.text: Close that track, fix the rail and run trains on the other track
options.result: Trains share the second track at a gentler pace, and the rail is fixed by nine. Passengers arrive 20 minutes late, but safely, and they know why.
options.lesson: Deal with danger first, then find the cleverest way to keep things moving.

options.text: Buy a measuring train that checks rails with sound waves every night
options.result: The measuring train finds tiny cracks months before they grow. Repairs become planned night jobs instead of morning surprises.
options.lesson: Finding problems early is cheaper than fixing them in a hurry.

options.text: Refund every delayed passenger automatically, without being asked
options.result: Money appears in passengers' accounts before they even ask. Many post that they've never been treated so well after a delay.
options.lesson: A quick sorry, without being asked, turns a bad morning into trust.

options.text: Stop Isla's bonus for causing a delay
options.result: Other engineers learn that reporting problems gets you punished. Next time, nobody says a word, and that is far more dangerous.
options.lesson: Thank the people who report problems, or they'll stop reporting them.

cases.title: The holiday rush
cases.story: Everyone wants to travel home for the holidays, and your trains are sold out two weeks early. Each of your 16 trains carries 1,000 people. A manager suggests selling standing tickets so every train can carry 1,500.

options.text: Add extra carriages, plus early-morning and late-night trains
options.result: Longer trains and extra early and late runs carry thousands more people a day. Families get home for the holidays, and your trains earn record money.
options.lesson: When demand is huge, add room safely instead of squeezing more people in.

options.text: Sell standing tickets so 1,500 people can squeeze onto each train
options.result: The carriages are so packed that nobody can reach the doors. Safety inspectors stop it on day two and fine you, and angry videos fill the internet.
options.lesson: A train has a safe number of passengers for a reason: never squeeze in more.

options.text: Raise prices a little at the busiest times, keep cheap early tickets
options.result: Some people travel a day earlier to save money, which spreads the crowds out. Busy trains earn a bit more, and nobody feels ripped off.
options.lesson: A fair price change can spread out the crowds and earn you more.

options.text: Sell joint tickets with the airport: land, then zoom home by train
options.result: Travellers book one ticket for plane and train together. Your airport station gets busier all year round, not just in the holidays.
options.lesson: Partners who carry the same travellers can grow together.

options.text: Triple the prices: people will pay anything to get home
options.result: You earn more this week, but families feel cheated. Many fly next time, and newspapers call you 'the greedy railway'.
options.lesson: Taking advantage of people when they need you most loses their trust for years.

businesses.pitch: A studio with giant sound stages where crews make films and TV programmes.
businesses.earns: Cinemas pay a share of every ticket, streaming services pay to show your films, and toys and games of your characters earn more.
businesses.costs: Actors, directors and big crews, building sets, special effects, music, advertising, and running the giant stages and cameras.
businesses.risks: A film costing millions can flop, a star can quit, filming can run late and over budget, and people can copy films illegally.
businesses.tip: Nobody knows which film will be a hit, so make several at sensible budgets rather than risking everything on one giant film.

cases.title: Lights, camera, budget!
cases.story: It's your studio's first year. Director Kemi wants the whole budget for one giant space adventure. Your team suggests four smaller films instead: a comedy, a nature film, a cartoon and a mystery. Between films, your sound stages (filming halls) will sit empty.

options.text: Make four smaller films, so one flop can't sink the studio
options.result: The mystery flops, but the cartoon is a surprise hit and the comedy does well. Together the four films make a healthy profit.
options.lesson: When you can't know which idea will win, try several instead of one.

options.text: Give Kemi the whole budget for one giant space film
options.result: The space film looks amazing but opens the same week as a superhero film. Few people come, and the whole year's money is gone.
options.lesson: Risking everything on one big idea can lose everything at once.

options.text: Rent your empty stages to TV companies between your films
options.result: A cooking programme and a quiz show rent your empty stages. Their rent pays the bills even in months with no film.
options.lesson: Steady income from what you already own makes a risky business much calmer.

options.text: Show early versions to test audiences and fix the boring bits
options.result: At a test screening, children fidget during a long talking scene. You cut it, and the finished cartoon keeps everyone laughing.
options.lesson: Let real customers try your product before it's finished.

options.text: Insure every film against accidents, delays and bad weather
options.result: A storm flattens an outdoor set halfway through filming. The insurance pays to rebuild it, so the film still finishes on budget.
options.lesson: In a business full of surprises, insurance turns big shocks into small ones.

cases.title: The star wants more
cases.story: Your big film starts in two weeks. Its star, Jasper Lane, now wants $10 million instead of the $3 million agreed, or he'll walk away. The whole film was planned around him, and his agent says: 'Every studio wants him.'

options.text: Offer the agreed fee plus a share of the profit if it's a hit
options.result: Jasper likes the idea of sharing in a hit. He signs, the film does well, and you both earn more than you expected.
options.lesson: Sharing the reward when things go well can beat paying a fortune up front.

options.text: Pay him what he asks: the film needs him
options.result: Jasper signs, but now the film must earn far more just to cover its costs. Other actors hear about it and ask for more too.
options.lesson: Giving in to every demand makes the next demand bigger.

options.text: Cast a talented new actor, and spend the savings on the story
options.result: Newcomer Ana Silva is brilliant, and audiences love discovering a fresh face. The film costs less and earns plenty.
options.lesson: A great story with a new face can shine as brightly as a famous name.

options.text: Ask your lawyer to check what Jasper already signed
options.result: Your lawyer finds that Jasper signed a contract for $3 million months ago. His agent backs down, and filming starts on time.
options.lesson: Check what was agreed before you argue: a signed contract is a strong friend.

options.text: Spread a false story that he's rude, so other studios won't hire him
options.result: Reporters trace the story back to your studio. Jasper takes you to court, and other stars refuse to work with a studio that spreads lies.
options.lesson: Spreading lies about someone to win an argument always comes back on you.

cases.title: A streaming giant calls
cases.story: Your cartoon is a hit! A streaming service (a website that shows films whenever you like) offers $25 million to own it for ever, with every sequel, toy and game. A toy company would rather make the toys and pay you a share of each one sold.

options.text: Keep owning it: let the streaming service show it for five years
options.result: The streaming service pays $8 million to show it for five years. You keep the characters, and the sequel and the toys earn you far more.
options.lesson: Rent out what you've made, but think twice before selling it for ever.

options.text: Let the toy company make the toys, for a share of each one sold
options.result: Your characters fill the toy shops at Christmas. A small share of millions of toys adds up to a big cheque.
options.lesson: A hit can earn far more than tickets if you let others make things from it, for a fee.

options.text: Check that the toy factories are safe and fair before signing
options.result: One factory's paint fails a safety test. You pick a safer factory, and parents trust toys with your characters on them.
options.lesson: Your characters carry your name, so make sure everything with them on is safe.

options.text: Tell the buyers your cartoon earned twice what it really did
options.result: The streaming service checks the cinema figures, which anyone can look up. It walks away and tells everyone you can't be trusted.
options.lesson: Never puff up your numbers: buyers check them, and lost trust is hard to win back.

options.text: Sell it for ever for $25 million: money now is safest
options.result: The money is nice, but the sequels and toys go on to earn the streaming service $100 million. You own none of it.
options.lesson: Selling your best idea for ever can cost you everything it earns later.

businesses.pitch: A giant holiday resort by the sea, with hotels, pools, beaches and fun for every age.
businesses.earns: Guests pay for rooms, meals, boat trips, kids' clubs and activities. Summer and school holidays bring the biggest crowds.
businesses.costs: Thousands of staff, food, water, power, cleaning, lifeguards, repairs, marketing and paying back the building loan.
businesses.risks: Storms and rainy summers, a bad review spreading online, a food scare, quiet winters, and harm to the reef or beach guests come for.
businesses.tip: Guests come for the place and come back for the people: protect the beach and the reef, and train your staff to be kind.

cases.title: Building by the reef
cases.story: Your $50 million resort will stand on a sunny island, by a bay with a coral reef (a living underwater garden full of fish). Builders want to blast a channel through the reef for speedboats. Local fishing families worry about their catch, and you need 2,000 staff.

options.text: Protect the reef, and hire fishing families as snorkel guides
options.result: The reef stays alive, and local fishing families become snorkel guides. Guests say swimming with turtles was the best day of their holiday.
options.lesson: Protect the thing your customers come for, and it keeps paying you back.

options.text: Hire and train local people first, with fair pay and promotions
options.result: Nearly half your staff come from nearby villages. They know the island, guests love their stories, and few of them leave.
options.lesson: When your neighbours work with you, the whole area wants you to succeed.

options.text: Collect rainwater and use solar power for the pools and lights
options.result: Sunshine powers your pools, and rainwater fills them. Your bills shrink, and guests like staying somewhere that cares for the island.
options.lesson: Saving water and power is good for nature and for your monthly bills.

options.text: Insure the resort against storms and floods
options.result: When a storm tears tiles off the roof and floods the lobby, the insurer pays for the repairs, and you reopen within a week.
options.lesson: By the sea, storms are a matter of when, not if: insurance is part of the plan.

options.text: Blast the channel so speedboats can zoom right up to the beach
options.result: The blasting destroys much of the reef. The fish vanish, the fishing families are angry, and snorkellers find only grey rubble.
options.lesson: Wrecking what makes a place special to save a few minutes is a bad trade.

cases.title: A tummy bug
cases.story: Forty guests catch a tummy bug in one week. Your kitchen manager, Lucia, thinks the lunch buffet sat out in the hot sun for too long. A travel website is asking questions, and the health inspectors arrive on Friday.

options.text: Tell guests it's just sunstroke and keep the buffet going
options.result: More guests fall ill. The inspectors find the warm buffet, close your kitchens for a week and fine you, and the 'sunstroke' story makes it worse.
options.lesson: Hiding the cause of a problem lets it spread; being honest lets you fix it.

options.text: Close the buffet, deep-clean the kitchens and tell guests honestly
options.result: Fresh food cooked to order replaces the warm buffet. Within three days nobody new is ill, and guests thank you for being straight with them.
options.lesson: When customers' health is at stake, act fast and be honest.

options.text: Retrain every cook to keep food cold, hot and covered
options.result: Cooks learn the food-safety rules, with checks every hour. When the inspectors visit, they give your kitchens top marks.
options.lesson: Good habits, checked every day, stop problems from coming back.

options.text: Refund the ill guests' stay and phone each one to say sorry
options.result: Guests are surprised the boss called them personally. Several book again for next summer, and one writes a glowing review.
options.lesson: A real sorry, with action, can turn an upset guest into a loyal one.

options.text: Wait and see if it stops on its own
options.result: It doesn't stop. By the weekend, 80 guests are ill, and a travel website warns people not to book.
options.lesson: A health problem doesn't fix itself: the sooner you act, the smaller it stays.

cases.title: A famous online star
cases.story: Sunny Day, an online star with 20 million followers, offers to film her family's holiday at your resort in return for a free week. 'And don't worry,' she says, 'I won't say it's an advert. Fans trust it more that way.'

options.text: Agree, if her videos say clearly that it's an advert
options.result: Sunny's family has a wonderful week, and every video says 'advert' at the start. Bookings still jump, because the resort really is lovely.
options.lesson: Honest adverts work when your product is good: you don't need to hide them.

options.text: Agree to keep it secret: fans trust it more that way
options.result: Hiding that a post is an advert breaks the rules. Fans find out, the videos are taken down, and you're fined.
options.lesson: Customers have a right to know when something is an advert: hiding it is a trick.

options.text: Invite real guests to share honest reviews after their stay
options.result: Hundreds of families post their real photos and stories. New guests trust them, because they're real people with no reason to fib.
options.lesson: Happy real customers are the most believable adverts of all.

options.text: Check whether her fans are families like your guests
options.result: Most of Sunny's fans are families who love beach holidays: just your kind of guest. Now you know the deal is worth doing.
options.lesson: Before you give anything for an advert, check it reaches the people you want.

options.text: Pay her to post about the resort every week for a year
options.result: Her fans get bored of the same resort every week, and the comments turn grumpy. A whole year of posts costs a fortune for little extra.
options.lesson: More of a good thing isn't always better: too many adverts annoy people.

businesses.pitch: A giant indoor arena where 20,000 fans watch concerts, ice shows and big matches.
businesses.earns: Bands and shows pay to use the arena, and you earn from tickets, snacks, T-shirts and parking on every big night.
businesses.costs: Staff for every show, security, cleaning up after 20,000 fans, sound and lighting gear, power, insurance and the building loan.
businesses.risks: Empty nights with no shows, a star cancelling at the last minute, crowd safety problems, fake tickets, and a newer arena nearby.
businesses.tip: Keep the calendar full and the crowds safe: an arena with a great show most nights, and fans who get home safely, earns all year.

cases.title: Filling the calendar
cases.story: Your 20,000-seat arena opens in autumn, and its calendar is empty. A big music promoter (a company that organises tours) offers 40 concerts a year if it gets all the snack money. A local ice-hockey team wants home matches, and schools want a big end-of-year show.

options.text: Mix it up: concerts, hockey, ice shows and school events all year
options.result: Your calendar fills up: concerts at weekends, hockey on weeknights and school shows in summer. The arena is busy nearly every night.
options.lesson: Lots of different customers keep you busy all year, and safe if one leaves.

options.text: Sign the promoter, but keep half the snack money
options.result: The promoter grumbles, then agrees. Forty concerts a year fill the arena, and half the snack money is still a mountain of popcorn.
options.lesson: A big partner is worth having, but negotiate the part that earns you most.

options.text: Plan safe ways in and out: wide exits, stewards and clear signs
options.result: Stewards in bright jackets guide fans in and out, and 20,000 people leave in 15 minutes. Families feel safe bringing their children.
options.lesson: With huge crowds, safety planning is the most important show of all.

options.text: Ask the train company to run late trains after big shows
options.result: Extra late trains wait for fans after every big show. The roads stay clear, and people know they can get home easily.
options.lesson: Think about your customers' whole night out, including the trip home.

options.text: Give the promoter every date and all the snack money
options.result: The promoter fills your dates and keeps the snack money. When it moves its tours to a newer arena, your calendar empties overnight.
options.lesson: If one partner controls your calendar, it controls your future.

cases.title: Fake tickets at the door
cases.story: Concert night! Pop star Nova is about to sing to a full arena. Outside, 1,500 fans hold fake tickets bought from a scam website, and some are in tears. Your doors manager says: 'We could squeeze them into the aisles and on the stairs.'

options.text: Squeeze them into the aisles and stairs: they're fans too
options.result: With the aisles blocked, nobody could get out quickly in an emergency. The safety officer stops the show for an hour, and your licence is suspended.
options.lesson: A safe crowd limit is never a guess: blocked exits put everyone at risk.

options.text: Keep to the safe limit, and help the tricked fans report the scam
options.result: Staff hand out hot chocolate and help fans report the scam website to the police. Nova records a video message for them, and many buy real tickets for her next tour.
options.lesson: Kindness and safety can go together, even when you have to say no.

options.text: Sell tickets only in your own app, with codes that can't be copied
options.result: Each ticket's code changes every few seconds, so a screenshot is useless. At the next big show, not a single fake gets through.
options.lesson: Make the honest way easy and the cheating way impossible.

options.text: Offer the tricked fans cheaper tickets for Nova's next show
options.result: It wasn't your fault, but you helped anyway. Next time Nova plays, those fans come back with real tickets and huge smiles.
options.lesson: Helping people who were tricked, even when it's not your fault, builds loyal fans.

options.text: Tell the fans it's their own fault and close the gates
options.result: The fans leave upset and post angry videos about your arena. Being right doesn't stop you looking unkind.
options.lesson: Even when you're in the right, how you treat people decides how they remember you.

cases.title: The world tour comes to town
cases.story: The world's biggest band wants to play five nights at your arena next summer: 100,000 tickets to sell. A ticket company offers to sell them, and suggests a 'booking fee' that appears only at the very last step of buying. 'Everyone does it,' they say.

options.text: Book all five nights, and show the full price from the start
options.result: Fans see one honest price, with no nasty surprise at the end. All five nights sell out in an hour, and fans praise your fair system.
options.lesson: Honest prices from the start build trust, and trust sells out shows.

options.text: Add the surprise fee at the last step: everyone does it
options.result: Fans feel tricked and complain to the consumer watchdog (the people who protect shoppers). You're fined and must refund every fee.
options.lesson: Hiding part of the price until the end is a trick, and customers remember it.

options.text: Limit tickets to four per person so touts can't grab them all
options.result: Touts (people who buy tickets to resell at sky-high prices) are stuck, and real fans get the seats. The band thanks you for looking after its fans.
options.lesson: Protect your real customers from people who want to profit from them.

options.text: Plan extra stewards, first aid and late trains for all five nights
options.result: Five huge nights pass without a single serious problem. The band's manager says yours is the best-run arena of the whole tour.
options.lesson: Big events go smoothly when the planning is bigger than the problems.

options.text: Auction the tickets so fans bid against each other
options.result: Only the richest fans get in, and prices hit thousands of dollars. Fans and the band are furious, and newspapers call you greedy.
options.lesson: Squeezing every penny out of loyal fans costs you their trust.

businesses.pitch: A high-tech factory that builds robots for warehouses, car factories and hospitals.
businesses.earns: Companies buy or rent robots for thousands of dollars each, then pay every year for software updates, repairs and training.
businesses.costs: Engineers and programmers, motors, sensors and chips, testing every robot, the factory itself, and research into new robots.
businesses.risks: A fault that means calling robots back to fix them, a shortage of chips, hackers, rivals with cleverer robots, and fewer orders in hard times.
businesses.tip: Robots work next to people, so test every one until it's safe and reliable, then look after your customers long after the sale.

cases.title: Two hundred robot helpers
cases.story: Your first robots lift heavy boxes in warehouses, and each one costs $80,000 to make. A warehouse company wants 200 but can't pay $150,000 each up front. Your engineers also want time to teach the robots to stop whenever a person comes near.

options.text: Rent the robots by the month, with repairs and updates included
options.result: The warehouse rents all 200 robots for $3,000 a month each. In about two years they've paid for themselves, and they keep on earning.
options.lesson: Renting can win customers who can't pay up front, and gives you steady income.

options.text: Give the engineers time to perfect the stop-near-people sensors
options.result: In tests, a robot stops a hand's width from a worker who steps out from behind a shelf. Safety inspectors approve your robots straight away.
options.lesson: A robot that works near people must be safe before it is fast.

options.text: Train the warehouse staff to work alongside the robots
options.result: Workers learn to send robots on jobs from a tablet. The robots do the heavy lifting, and the people do the clever planning.
options.lesson: New machines work best when people understand them and feel part of the change.

options.text: Build 1,000 robots now, before any customer has tried one
options.result: After trying the first robots, the warehouse asks for a few changes. Now you have 1,000 robots to fix, and they fill your car park for months.
options.lesson: Let real customers try a product before you make it by the thousand.

options.text: Sell them cheaply at $90,000 each to beat any rival
options.result: You sell plenty but earn almost nothing on each. When robots need repairs, there's no money left to pay your engineers.
options.lesson: A price that barely covers your costs leaves nothing for surprises.

cases.title: The robot recall
cases.story: Your hospital robots carry medicines along corridors. Nurse Adebayo reports that one robot's brakes slipped on a wet floor. Your engineers find the same faulty part in all 300 robots you've sold. Calling them back to fix (a recall) would cost $3 million.

options.text: Say nothing, and swap the part only if a hospital complains
options.result: Another robot slips and knocks over a trolley of medicines. The hospitals learn you knew about the fault, and the safety authority fines you millions.
options.lesson: Hiding a safety fault you know about turns a mistake into a scandal.

options.text: Call back every robot, swap the part for free and tell hospitals why
options.result: Your engineers swap the part in all 300 robots within a month. Hospitals are so impressed by your honesty that they order 100 more.
options.lesson: Owning up to a fault and fixing it fast is how trust survives a mistake.

options.text: Add a wet-floor test to every robot's checks from now on
options.result: Your test track now has a slippery corner. Every new robot must stop safely on it before it leaves the factory.
options.lesson: Turn every mistake into a new test, so it never happens again.

options.text: Find out why the faulty part wasn't caught, and fix the cause
options.result: A supplier changed the brake material without telling you. Now every delivery of parts is tested before it's used.
options.lesson: Find the real cause, not just the broken part, and the problem stays fixed.

options.text: Blame the hospitals for having slippery floors
options.result: The hospitals are not impressed. Two cancel their orders, and the others start looking at rival robots.
options.lesson: Blaming your customers for your product's fault loses them fast.

cases.title: Fifty hospitals and a video deal
cases.story: Fifty hospitals want your robots, your biggest order yet, but you can only build 20 a month. Meanwhile, a tech company offers $5 million for the videos your robots' cameras record in hospital corridors, 'to teach our AI'.

options.text: Build a second robot-making line and deliver in planned stages
options.result: A second line doubles your output. Hospitals get their robots in a clear order, busiest first, and every delivery arrives on time.
options.lesson: Grow in planned steps, and keep every promise along the way.

options.text: Sell the hospital videos: the faces are blurry anyway
options.result: Patients never agreed to be filmed for a tech company. The hospitals cancel their orders, and the government's privacy office fines you millions.
options.lesson: People's private information isn't yours to sell, however blurry the pictures.

options.text: Switch off recording: robots need to see, not to keep videos
options.result: Your robots still see the corridor to steer, but nothing is saved. Hospitals love the promise, and it helps you win the order.
options.lesson: Collect only the information you truly need, and people will trust you more.

options.text: Train a team in each hospital to look after the robots
options.result: Each hospital gets two trained robot carers. Small problems are fixed in minutes, and your engineers spend less time on the road.
options.lesson: Helping customers care for what they bought saves everyone time and money.

options.text: Promise all 50 hospitals their robots next month
options.result: You can't build them that fast. Most hospitals get nothing on the promised day, and several cancel in frustration.
options.lesson: Promising what you can't deliver loses customers faster than saying 'not yet'.

businesses.pitch: A space company that launches and runs satellites for phones, maps and weather forecasts.
businesses.earns: Phone companies, map apps, weather services and ships pay every month to use your satellites' signals, pictures and data.
businesses.costs: Building satellites, paying for rocket launches, insurance, ground stations with giant dishes, and engineers who steer them.
businesses.risks: A failed launch, a satellite hit by space junk or a solar storm, hackers, and rivals launching thousands of cheaper satellites.
businesses.tip: In space you can't send a repair van, so test everything twice, insure every launch and never put everything on one rocket.

cases.title: Twelve satellites, one rocket?
cases.story: Your first 12 satellites will bring phone signal to ships and faraway villages. One big rocket could carry all 12 at once, or you could split them across three launches, which costs $4 million more. A parts maker also offers half-price parts never tested in space.

options.text: Split the satellites across three launches
options.result: A storm delays the first launch, but the other two go ahead, and your service starts on time. No single rocket ever carries your whole company.
options.lesson: Don't put all your eggs in one basket, or all your satellites on one rocket.

options.text: Insure every launch and each satellite's first year in space
options.result: The cover costs millions, which hurts. But if a rocket ever fails, you can build again instead of closing down.
options.lesson: When one accident could cost everything, insurance is part of the plan.

options.text: Sign up customers before launch, so the satellites earn from day one
options.result: A shipping company and an island phone company sign up early. The day your satellites switch on, money starts arriving.
options.lesson: Customers signed up before you launch make a risky start much safer.

options.text: Put all 12 on one rocket and save $4 million
options.result: A fault in the rocket's top stage leaves all 12 satellites in the wrong orbit. Every one is lost, and so is a whole year.
options.lesson: Saving money by risking everything on one launch can cost you everything.

options.text: Buy the half-price parts: they look exactly the same
options.result: Two satellites stop working in their first month, frozen by the bitter cold of space. Customers leave, and replacing them costs a fortune.
options.lesson: Parts that were never tested where they'll be used are a risk, not a bargain.

cases.title: Space junk ahead!
cases.story: An alarm sounds in your control room: an old, broken satellite is tumbling towards one of yours, with a 1-in-10 chance they crash in 30 hours. Dodging uses fuel and shortens your satellite's life by a few months. A crash would scatter thousands of bits of junk.

options.text: Nudge your satellite out of the way and warn other companies
options.result: A short engine burn moves your satellite to safety. The broken one tumbles past, and other companies thank you for sharing the warning.
options.lesson: When a small cost now avoids a huge disaster later, pay it.

options.text: Don't dodge: if they crash, the insurance will pay
options.result: The satellites collide, and the junk damages two more. The insurer refuses to pay because you ignored the warning, and space agencies fine you.
options.lesson: Insurance is for accidents you couldn't stop, not ones you chose not to.

options.text: Save fuel in every satellite to steer it down safely when it's old
options.result: Each satellite now keeps fuel for one last trip down, where it burns up harmlessly. Space agencies call you a model company.
options.lesson: Clean up after yourself, even in space.

options.text: Pay for a tracking service that warns you days earlier
options.result: Early warnings let you dodge with tiny, gentle nudges instead of big burns. Your satellites keep more fuel and work for longer.
options.lesson: The earlier you see a problem coming, the cheaper it is to avoid.

options.text: Move every one of your satellites, just in case
options.result: Every satellite burns precious fuel, though only one was in danger. Now they'll all wear out sooner, for nothing.
options.lesson: Act on the real danger: panicking about everything wastes what you need later.

cases.title: Phones from space
cases.story: The country's biggest phone company wants your satellites to send signal straight to ordinary phones, so nobody is ever cut off, even on mountains or at sea. It needs 50 more satellites and offers a 10-year deal, but wants to be your only customer.

options.text: Sign for 10 years, but keep the right to serve other customers
options.result: The phone company agrees. Its customers get signal on mountains and at sea, and you also sell signal to shipping firms and airlines.
options.lesson: Grow with a big partner, but keep your freedom to serve others.

options.text: Ask the phone company to pay part of the cost of the satellites
options.result: The phone company pays a quarter of the cost up front. Your loan is smaller, and it's as keen as you are to make the plan work.
options.lesson: A partner who puts money in shares the risk, and the effort.

options.text: Let anyone in danger make free emergency calls through your satellites
options.result: Months later, a family whose boat broke down far out at sea calls for help through your satellites. They're rescued, and the whole country hears your name.
options.lesson: Doing good with what you've built makes people proud to be your customers.

options.text: Agree to work only for them: one giant customer is plenty
options.result: It works, until the phone company demands a lower price, knowing you have nobody else to sell to.
options.lesson: If one customer is your only customer, they decide your price.

options.text: Borrow big and build 200 satellites, in case others want some too
options.result: Only the phone company signs up. The extra satellites circle the Earth with nobody paying for them, while your loan payments pile up.
options.lesson: Grow to fit real orders, not orders you're only hoping for.

businesses.pitch: A power plant that makes clean electricity for the whole city from sun, wind and waves.
businesses.earns: The city pays for every unit of electricity you make, on long contracts. Giant batteries sell stored power when it's worth most.
businesses.costs: Engineers, repairs to turbines and panels, undersea cables, giant batteries, insurance and paying back the loans for building it.
businesses.risks: Calm, cloudy weeks, storms damaging turbines, a broken undersea cable, and the city needing power when there's no sun or wind.
businesses.tip: Mix sun, wind and waves so one is always working, store spare power for later, and keep the lights on: that's what the city pays for.

cases.title: Sun, wind or waves?
cases.story: The city wants your plant to power 200,000 homes. Solar panels work on sunny days and wind turbines on windy ones. New wave machines work all the time, but nobody has tested them here. The city will sign a 20-year deal if you promise to keep the lights on.

options.text: Mix all three, plus giant batteries for calm, dark evenings
options.result: When the wind drops, the sun shines; when both rest, the waves and batteries take over. The lights never flicker, and the city signs for 20 years.
options.lesson: Mixing different sources means one is always working when another can't.

options.text: Test one row of wave machines before buying a hundred
options.result: The test row shows that seaweed clogs the machines. The makers add a simple filter, and the full set works beautifully.
options.lesson: Test something new on a small scale before you build it big.

options.text: Ask fishing crews where to put the turbines so the fish stay safe
options.result: The fishing crews show you where fish lay their eggs. You build elsewhere, and the turbines' bases become homes for crabs and mussels.
options.lesson: Ask the people who know a place best before you build in it.

options.text: Sign the 20-year contract at a fair, steady price
options.result: With 20 years of income promised, the bank lends to you cheaply. Every month the money arrives like clockwork.
options.lesson: A long, fair contract turns a big project into a steady income you can plan around.

options.text: Go all-in on wave machines: the newest must be the best
options.result: The untested machines break in the first winter storms. For weeks you can't keep your promise, and the city has to buy power elsewhere.
options.lesson: Newest isn't always best: never rely on something nobody has tested.

cases.title: Blackout in the storm
cases.story: A winter storm snaps the undersea cable from your wind turbines, and half the city loses power on the coldest night of the year. Hospitals switch to backup generators. Repairs at sea take a week, and the storm is still raging.

options.text: Send a repair boat out now, in the storm, to fix it faster
options.result: Giant waves damage the boat, and its crew has to be lifted off by a rescue helicopter. They're safe, but you're fined, and the cable is still broken.
options.lesson: Never put your people in danger to fix something faster.

options.text: Send your stored power to hospitals and care homes first
options.result: Your giant batteries keep hospitals, care homes and the waterworks running through the night. Then power returns to homes street by street.
options.lesson: In a crisis, put the most important needs first.

options.text: Lay a second cable on a different route as a backup
options.result: The second cable takes a year to lay. When the next storm snaps one, the other keeps the power flowing and nobody even notices.
options.lesson: For anything truly important, have a backup route.

options.text: Send families honest updates: which streets, when, and why
options.result: People know when their street's power is coming back. Neighbours check on older people nearby, and the city stays calm.
options.lesson: In a blackout, clear and honest updates are almost as welcome as the lights.

options.text: Wait for the storm to end before making any plan
options.result: For two days nobody knows what's happening. By the time you have a plan, people are furious and the council wants answers.
options.lesson: Plan while the crisis is happening: waiting makes everything worse.

cases.title: The steelworks and the broker
cases.story: A steelworks wants clean power from you for 15 years, if you add 20 more wind turbines. Each unit of clean power comes with a certificate proving it's green. A broker (a go-between) whispers: 'Sell each certificate twice, to two companies. Nobody checks.'

options.text: Build the turbines for the steelworks, with a fair 15-year deal
options.result: The new turbines spin, and the steelworks' furnaces run on clean power. Its 'green steel' sells for more, so both of you win.
options.lesson: Helping a customer solve its biggest problem can be your biggest opportunity.

options.text: Sell each certificate twice: double the money, and nobody checks
options.result: The national register spots the same certificate numbers twice. You're fined millions, and both companies cancel their deals.
options.lesson: Selling the same thing twice is cheating, and records catch it in the end.

options.text: Ask the steelworks to share the cost of the new turbines
options.result: The steelworks pays a fifth of the cost, because it wants clean power badly. Your loan is smaller and your risk is lower.
options.lesson: When a deal helps both sides, it's fair to share the cost of making it happen.

options.text: Report the broker's idea to the certificate register
options.result: The register thanks you: he had tried the same trick on other power plants. Your honest name makes buyers trust your certificates.
options.lesson: Reporting a cheat protects your business and everyone else's.

options.text: Say no: 20 more turbines sounds like too much work
options.result: A rival power company builds the turbines and signs the 15-year deal. Your plant stays the same size while the city's need for power grows.
options.lesson: A big, safe deal with a trusted customer is worth the extra work.

businesses.pitch: A giant glass dome with heated pools, a spiral slide and palms, open all year round.
businesses.earns: Tickets, family season passes, school lessons, hotel holiday packages, plus cafés and shops under the dome, in any weather.
businesses.costs: Energy to heat the water and the air, pool chemicals, safety checks, hundreds of staff and repayments on a huge loan.
businesses.risks: Energy prices jumping, a safety fault, a long closure for repairs, tricky contracts and a rival dome opening nearby.
businesses.tip: Energy and safety are your two big numbers: cut the energy bill with clever design, and never save money on safety checks.

cases.title: The $450,000 energy bill
cases.story: Heating the water and the air under the glass costs $450,000 a month. An energy seller offers a 10-year price '30% cheaper' if you sign today. An engineer proposes heat pumps (machines that move heat instead of burning fuel) and solar panels.

options.text: Sign the 10-year 'cheaper' energy deal today
options.result: Page 14 says the price jumps after two years, with a $6 million fee to leave early. By year three the bill is bigger than before, and you are stuck.
options.lesson: 'Sign today to save lots' is how people get locked in. Read every page.

options.text: Fit heat pumps and rooftop solar panels with the engineer's plan
options.result: Over a year the dome makes much of its own power and wastes far less heat. The energy bill falls by a third, and the green plan makes the news.
options.lesson: A big, one-off investment that cuts your biggest cost for years can beat any discount.

options.text: Ask three energy firms for bids and have a lawyer read every contract
options.result: The lawyer spots a hidden clause in two of the bids. The third firm gives a fair, flexible deal for five years.
options.lesson: Compare offers and pay an expert to read the small print before signing.

options.text: Cover the pools at night and set the air one degree cooler
options.result: Night covers keep the heat in, and nobody notices one degree. The bill shrinks a little straight away, for free.
options.lesson: Small habits that save energy every day add up to a lot over a year.

options.text: Turn the heating way down to save money
options.result: The water turns chilly, families leave early and write that the 'tropical' dome is cold. The lost tickets cost more than the energy you saved.
options.lesson: Do not save money on the thing customers came for.

cases.title: A crack in the spiral slide
cases.story: At the yearly national safety check, the inspector finds a hairline crack in the spiral slide's support. The slide must stay closed until it passes a new check. A contractor whispers: 'For $50,000 cash I'll patch it tonight and hand you a stamped pass.'

options.text: Pay the contractor $50,000 cash for a quick patch and a pass paper
options.result: The inspector sees that the paper is not real. The dome is closed for weeks, the contractor disappears, and the fines are huge.
options.lesson: A fake safety paper puts families in danger. Safety is never for sale.

options.text: Close the slide and let its maker's engineers rebuild the support
options.result: The slide reopens after three weeks with a real pass and a party. The rest of the dome stayed open, so most guests hardly noticed.
options.lesson: Fix the cause properly: a real pass is worth far more than the days you lose.

options.text: Hire an independent engineer to check every structure in the dome each year
options.result: The engineer finds two more small problems in the roof and a pool ladder. All are repaired before they matter.
options.lesson: Checks by someone who does not work for you give you the truth.

options.text: Start a daily check: two staff sign off every slide and pool before opening
options.result: Each morning two people walk the slides with a list and sign it. A loose bolt is found and fixed within the first week.
options.lesson: Two people signing a checklist every day stops small faults becoming big ones.

options.text: Close the whole dome for a month to be extra safe
options.result: Hundreds of staff are paid to wait, season-pass holders are cross, and only one slide had a problem.
options.lesson: Close what is really unsafe. Shutting everything costs a fortune and fixes nothing more.

cases.title: Swim lessons and a fast loan
cases.story: The government offers $3 million a year to teach every 9-year-old in the region to swim on quiet weekday mornings. A fast-cash lender offers $30 million for a second dome at 1% a month (about 13% a year), to be signed today.

options.text: Accept the swim-lesson contract and teach on quiet weekday mornings
options.result: Certified teachers run lessons while the pools were empty anyway. Thousands of children learn to swim, and their families return at weekends.
options.lesson: Use your quiet hours for a reliable customer, and you can do good while earning well.

options.text: Ask your bank for a smaller, cheaper loan to add a toddler pool and café
options.result: The bank charges about 6% a year. The new pool is full of toddlers and parents, who buy lunch in the café.
options.lesson: Compare what each loan really costs in a year, and borrow only what you can repay.

options.text: Offer lesson families a cheaper off-peak family pass
options.result: Many parents of the new swimmers buy the pass and visit on quiet weekday afternoons. Those hours were once empty.
options.lesson: Turn a first-time visitor into a regular one with a pass that suits them.

options.text: Say no to both and keep the dome just as it is
options.result: Nothing goes wrong, and nothing grows. A rival dome signs the swim-lesson contract instead.
options.lesson: Saying no to everything is safe, but good chances rarely come twice.

options.text: Take the fast lender's $30 million now and build a second dome
options.result: Fees hidden in the small print make the loan dearer than it looked. The repayments squeeze the first dome, and the second is late.
options.lesson: A huge loan signed in a hurry can sink a business: add up everything you will pay back.

businesses.pitch: A giant stadium for league matches, cup finals and concerts, with a big screen.
businesses.earns: Clubs and promoters pay to use it, and you earn from tickets, food, drinks, corporate boxes, TV rights and the stadium's name.
businesses.costs: Stewards and safety staff, pitch care, floodlight and energy bills, cleaning, repairs, insurance and the huge loan on the building.
businesses.risks: A crowd safety problem, empty weekends, a cancelled event, ticket scams aimed at fans, a damaged pitch and angry neighbours.
businesses.tip: Fill the calendar with different events, but never let a crowd grow past the safe limit: safety comes before every ticket sold.

cases.title: The empty weekends
cases.story: Your 60,000-seat stadium opens soon. League clubs will play here on only 20 weekends a year, but the loan bill arrives every month. A concert promoter, a bank that wants to buy the stadium's name, and the city's schools all want dates.

options.text: Mix league games, concerts and school finals, each with its own safety plan
options.result: The calendar fills with league games, big concerts and the schools' cup day. Every event has a tested plan for exits, stewards and first aid, so crowds get home safely.
options.lesson: Many kinds of events fill the calendar, and a safety plan for each one keeps crowds safe.

options.text: Hire the stadium to the concert promoter for ten big weekends
options.result: Ten sold-out concerts bring in millions, and the contract makes the promoter pay for repairing the pitch afterwards.
options.lesson: A big hire deal is great when the contract covers the damage it can cause.

options.text: Sell the stadium's name, after checking who the sponsor is
options.result: The bank has a clean record and a good name with fans. The naming deal pays millions a year, and soon everyone uses the new name.
options.lesson: Your name will be linked to a sponsor's name, so check them before you sign.

options.text: Open stadium tours and a museum on quiet days
options.result: Visitors walk down the tunnel, stand by the pitch and see the trophy room. The tours earn a little every day and make fans of people who never came to a match.
options.lesson: Empty days can earn money too, if you give people a reason to visit.

options.text: Let any group hire the stadium without asking what they plan to do
options.result: A crowded event with no plan blocks the exits and upsets the neighbours. The city warns you that your licence to hold big events is at risk.
options.lesson: Saying yes to everyone can cost you the licence that lets you earn at all.

cases.title: Cup final fever
cases.story: Cup final week! The safe limit is 60,000 people, but 90,000 fans want tickets. Online resellers already sell fake tickets at five times the price, and a club director says: 'Just sell 5,000 extra. Who will count?'

options.text: Keep to 60,000, name every ticket and open a face-price swap page
options.result: Only real fans get in, and those who cannot come swap their tickets safely at the printed price. Resellers lose their business and fans thank you online.
options.lesson: Protect fans from scammers by making the real way easy and the fake way useless.

options.text: Sell 5,000 extra tickets: some fans will not turn up anyway
options.result: Everyone turns up. The stairways jam, stewards cannot reach some seats and the safety officer delays the match. You refund thousands of fans and pay a fine.
options.lesson: The safe limit is set so everyone gets out safely, so it is never a target to beat.

options.text: Ask the railway for extra trains and the council for match-day bus lanes
options.result: Fans stream to and from the stadium by train and bus. The nearby streets stay calm and the neighbours stop complaining about parked cars.
options.lesson: Getting fans to and from the stadium is part of the show.

options.text: Warn fans in every message to buy only from the official website
options.result: Many fans learn to check the web address, so fewer are caught by fakes. Your helpline answers hundreds of calls from fans checking a ticket.
options.lesson: Teaching customers to spot fakes protects them and protects your name.

options.text: Ignore the resellers: fake tickets are not your problem
options.result: Hundreds of fans with fake tickets are turned away at the gates, in tears. They blame the stadium, not the scammers.
options.lesson: Protecting your customers from scams is part of your job, even when you are not the cheat.

cases.title: The new roof
cases.story: Rain soaks 20,000 seats and fans leave early. A new roof costs $12 million. A lender offers the whole loan tonight at a very low rate, but the contract is 90 pages long. Your floodlights also cost $90,000 a month in power.

options.text: Have a lawyer read the loan, ask for a fixed rate and apply for a city grant
options.result: The lawyer finds the rate would have jumped after two years. You win a fixed rate, and the city adds a grant because the roof also shelters fans in storms.
options.lesson: Read the contract, negotiate it and look for help before you borrow big.

options.text: Sign the loan tonight before the offer disappears
options.result: On page 74 the rate triples after two years, and the bank may take the stadium if one payment is late. The repayments swallow your profit.
options.lesson: A deal that cannot wait until tomorrow is a deal to be wary of.

options.text: Swap the floodlights for LEDs so the power bill shrinks
options.result: The new lights use far less power, switch on instantly and look sharper on TV. The saving pays back their cost in about four years.
options.lesson: A cost that pays itself back in a few years is an investment, not just a spend.

options.text: Roof the busiest stands first and the rest later
options.result: Fans in the covered stands stay dry, and the smaller loan is easier to repay. You can build the rest when the money is ready.
options.lesson: Building a big project in steps keeps the debt small and the risk lower.

options.text: Skip the roof and hand out rain ponchos
options.result: Fans in the wet stands call it a joke, and fewer buy seats there. The leaks get worse and the repair bill grows.
options.lesson: Putting off a big repair usually makes the repair bigger.
